body.statement: For every instance in \(\mathfrak M_{\mathrm{exp}}\) whose undirected full graph \(G\) has exactly one cycle, the two-arc reachability augmentation specified by \(\operatorname{UnicycleHandle}\) yields a sound-and-complete polynomial-size certificate calculus and a polynomial-time min-sum algorithm.  It decides whether \(X=a_X\) is a Beckers actual cause of \(Y=a_Y\), computes the minimum nonnegative rational deletion cost when a witness exists, and returns either a replayable attaining witness or replayable separating dynamic-program tables.  The running time is polynomial in \(L\), and exact cost operations have polynomial bit complexity in \(L+B\).
body.proof_tex:
Let \(C\) be the unique undirected cycle of \(G\).  We first isolate the entire nonlocal part of deletion legality.  If an edge \(e=p\to Z\) is not on \(C\), there is no second undirected route between \(p\) and \(Z\), so deletion of \(e\) can never leave a directed \(p\)-to-\(Z\) path.  If \(e\) lies on \(C\), its only possible alternative route is \(C\setminus\{e\}\).  Call \(e\) dangerous when every edge of that complementary route is oriented from \(p\) toward \(Z\).  There is at most one dangerous edge: if \(e\) has this property, the orientation on all other cycle edges is fixed along the complementary \(p\)-to-\(Z\) route, and removing any other edge exposes, on its complementary route, one segment traversed against that orientation.  Therefore, for every retained subgraph \(H\),
\[
 H\in\mathcal H(G)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \neg\bigl(\delta_e=1\ \text{and}\ \delta_f=0\text{ for every }f\in C\setminus\{e\}\bigr)
\]
when a dangerous edge \(e\) exists, where \(\delta_f=1\) denotes deletion; if none exists, every deletion pattern is graphically legal.  Indeed, the forward implication is the definition of legality, and the reverse implication follows because the preceding argument lists every edge that can possibly have an alternative retained path.  Thus the full reachability obligation is recognized by the two-bit signature
\[
 \bigl(\delta_e,\rho\bigr),
 \qquad
 \rho=\mathbf 1\{\delta_f=0\text{ for all }f\in C\setminus\{e\}\},
\]
with the single rejecting signature \((1,1)\).  Equivalently one may carry the two arc-intactness bits while walking around the cut cycle.  This is the finite reachability state prescribed by \(\operatorname{UnicycleHandle}\).

We now give an explicit finite optimization whose feasible records are exactly the causal witnesses.  For each edge \(p\to Z\), retain its deletion bit \(\delta_{pZ}\), and put
\[
 D_Z=\{p\in\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z):\delta_{pZ}=1\},
 \qquad S_Z=\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)\setminus D_Z.
\]
For every \(Z\ne X\), define the local relation on alternate values \(v_Z\) and \(v_{\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)}\) to hold when
\[
 Q_Z^{S_Z}(a_{S_Z})=\{a_Z\}
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \exists r\in R(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z)):
 r|_{S_Z}=v|_{S_Z},\quad v_Z\in A_Z(r).
\]
For \(Z=X\), retain only the first condition, because intervention replaces its alternate structural equation.  Add the unary requirements \(v_U=a_U\), \(v_X\ne a_X\), and \(v_Y\ne a_Y\), and charge the local amount \(\sum_{p\in D_Z}c(p\to Z)\).

By \texttt{lem:canonical-replay}, every feasible collection of these local records whose two-bit signature is not rejecting determines a legal structural simplification and a complete alternate solution changing \(Y\); the displayed supporting rows are precisely the witnesses for projected membership.  Conversely, every Beckers witness supplies its deletion bits, alternate values, and one such supporting row at each nonintervened node, and its graphical legality gives an accepted signature.  The sum of local charges counts every deleted edge exactly once.  Consequently the minimum of this finite constraint system equals the minimum deletion cost over canonical Beckers witnesses, rather than merely defining a surrogate functional.

It remains to solve the constraint system in polynomial time.  Form a bipartite factor graph with a value vertex for each variable and a factor vertex \(f_Z\) for each endogenous table; join \(f_Z\) to \(Z\) and to every parent of \(Z\).  This operation adds one factor vertex and one extra incidence edge for each endogenous vertex while replacing every original parent edge by one parent-factor incidence.  It preserves connected components and cycle rank, since
\[
 (|E(G)|+|V|)-(|U|+2|V|)+\#\operatorname{components}
 =|E(G)|-(|U|+|V|)+\#\operatorname{components}.
\]
Hence the factor graph also has exactly one cycle.

The local factor tables can be generated in polynomial time from the explicit input.  For a node \(Z\), enumerate alternate parent tuples, candidate supporting rows, output incidences, and deletion masks.  An off-cycle parent with singleton domain never needs deletion: its projection is unchanged, its deletion cannot repair cycle legality, and its cost is nonnegative.  Apart from at most two incoming cycle edges, every enumerated deletion coordinate therefore has a domain of size at least two.  If \(N_Z=|R(\operatorname{Pa}_G(Z))|\) is the explicitly supplied number of parent rows, the number of relevant masks is at most
\[
 4\,2^{\#\{p:|R(p)|\ge2\}}\le4N_Z.
\]
For each mask, the actual-row equality is checked by scanning the explicit rows, exactly as in \texttt{lem:local-hitting-equivalence}; supporting membership is checked by another finite scan.  Thus even the direct nested enumeration is bounded by a fixed polynomial in \(L\).  It records the minimum local rational charge for each boundary value tuple and each choice of the at most two incident cycle-deletion bits.

Cut one incidence edge of the unique factor-graph cycle.  The remainder is a forest.  Enumerate the common value on the two copies of the cut boundary and the initial two-bit reachability signature.  On every attached tree compute min-sum messages from leaves inward.  A variable-to-factor message at value \(v\) is the sum of incoming child messages; a factor-to-variable message is the minimum, over the other incident values and the factor's explicit local records, of the local charge plus those child messages.  Along the opened cycle, update \(\rho\) by conjunction with retention of the next cycle edge and carry \(\delta_e\) when the dangerous edge is encountered.  At closure require equality of the duplicated boundary value and reject \((\delta_e,\rho)=(1,1)\).  Unary actual, intervention, and outcome constraints are imposed at their value vertices.

Induction on the number of eliminated factor-graph vertices proves the message invariant: each table entry is the minimum charge of all assignments in the eliminated component having the displayed boundary value and reachability signature.  The leaf case is the corresponding local factor entry; the variable and factor recurrences partition all extensions by their boundary values, so taking sums over disjoint factors and minima over internal values proves the induction step.  Closure therefore returns finite value exactly for a feasible global record, and its least finite value is the exact witness optimum established above.  Stored argmin pointers reconstruct all deletion bits, alternate values, and supporting rows.

The local tables and all message arrays have polynomial size because their value domains and mask lists are bounded by the explicit row counts.  A positive certificate consists of the reconstructed record.  A negative certificate consists of the finite factor tables and all message arrays ending with no accepted closure entry; an optimality certificate adds the argmin pointers.  A verifier regenerates each local entry and checks every displayed min-sum recurrence and the final signature condition.  The same induction proves soundness and completeness of these certificates.  The number of exact arithmetic operations is polynomial in \(L\).  Finally, each candidate cost is a sum of at most \(L\) nonnegative rationals; the common-denominator argument from \texttt{thm:compiler-verifier-equivalence} bounds every scaled integer by \(O(B+\log(L+1))\) bits.  Hence verification and optimization have polynomial bit complexity in \(L+B\).  This proves the positive alternative posed by the open-ended question.
